title: India Pays Above $23 per MMBtu for LNG as Iran War Drives Prices to Multi-Year Highs
excerpt: GAIL India and Gujarat State Petroleum Corp. have purchased September delivery cargoes at the highest spot prices since 2022, as the Middle East conflict continues to disrupt global supply routes.
body:
• Indian energy companies are paying above $23 per MMBtu for September LNG cargoes, the highest spot import prices since 2022, as the Iran war disrupts supply through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • GAIL India, Gujarat State Petroleum Corp., and Bharat Petroleum have all bought spot LNG cargoes at elevated prices to cover shortfalls from lost Qatari supply.
  • India has diversified away from Qatar — which supplied 45% of its LNG in 2025 — by increasing imports from the US (sixfold increase), Nigeria, Oman, and Angola.
  • Record power demand driven by extreme heat and a solar-storage gap is forcing India to buy expensive LNG for nighttime peaking generation, even at commercially unattractive prices.

Spot Prices Surge Past $23

Indian energy companies are paying more than $23 per million British thermal units for LNG cargoes scheduled for September delivery, among the highest spot import prices since 2022, according to a Bloomberg report on August 21. GAIL India, the country's largest gas distributor, and Gujarat State Petroleum Corp. have both purchased cargoes at these levels. Bharat Petroleum has also entered the spot market.

The purchases come as the ongoing Iran war continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for global energy trade. Asian LNG benchmark prices (JKM) have surged from a pre-crisis $10.4 per MMBtu to $25.3 by late March, before easing to around $16-18 in recent months. The latest Indian purchases at $23-plus signal a renewed tightening as fresh escalation between the US and Iran has rattled shipping confidence.

Ship-tracking service MarineTraffic reported that vessel activity through the Strait of Hormuz declined by approximately 52% week-on-week in mid-July, with traffic shifting toward more defensive routing patterns.

Replacing Qatar's Missing Supply

India's LNG procurement has been upended since the conflict disrupted Qatari production in early March. Qatar accounted for 11.2 million tonnes of India's 25 million tonnes of LNG imports in 2025 — roughly 45% of total supply. State firm QatarEnergy declared force majeure on deliveries after its Ras Laffan complex, the world's largest LNG export facility, was damaged.

India has responded by rapidly diversifying its supply base. US LNG exports to India increased more than sixfold, from 137,000 tonnes in January to 907,000 tonnes in May, making the US India's largest LNG supplier. Nigeria doubled its monthly shipments to 480,000 tonnes, while Oman averaged around 500,000 tonnes per month in March and April. Angola and Algeria have also emerged as new sources.

"Gas availability at the moment is not a matter of concern. You just need to pay the higher prices. If one can pay around $17-18 per MMBtu, you would have the gas. It's an issue of pricing."

— Rajesh K. Mediratta, MD and CEO, Indian Gas Exchange

Heat, Solar Gap, and the Need for Expensive Gas

India's renewed LNG buying is driven not by structural gas demand but by the weather. Power consumption jumped more than 11% year-on-year to 164.98 billion kWh in May 2026 as temperatures exceeded 45°C across large parts of the country. Peak power demand hit records on four consecutive days from May 17-21, reaching an all-time high of 270.82 GW on May 21.

The crisis has exposed a central weakness in India's fast-evolving power system: installed solar capacity reached 154.2 GW by April 2026, pushing daytime electricity prices toward zero. But battery storage has not kept pace, leaving a gap when the sun goes down. Cities remain hot at night, cooling demand stays elevated, and prices spike. On the day of the historic demand record, India still faced a 2.5 GW nighttime shortfall.

Gas-fired power plants, which contribute just about 10 GW during high-demand periods from a maximum capacity of roughly 20 GW, are being pulled into service as emergency peaking capacity. In early April, India's Ministry of Power directed all gas-based generation stations to be ready to operate during heatwave shortages. The government arrangement allows Grid-India to pre-define operational hours several days in advance.

Why India Cannot Stop Buying

While high LNG prices have triggered demand destruction across much of Asia — South Korea cut imports by 1 million tonnes per month between February and April, Japan by 1.5 million tonnes — India moved in the opposite direction. After dipping to 1.67 million tonnes in March, Indian LNG imports climbed to 2.1 million tonnes in May.

Coal plants are already carrying most of the load, with about 2.1 GW of coal-fired capacity currently unavailable due to maintenance. Hydropower's timing is poor: reservoirs are partly depleted in the late pre-monsoon period, and a Super Niño phenomenon is forecast to weaken the monsoon, potentially dragging rainfall to its lowest level in 11 years.

That leaves LNG as the marginal fuel of India's summer power crisis. India can theoretically double gas-fired generation from 10 GW to 20 GW. Until New Delhi can store its solar boom and the monsoon delivers relief, it will keep paying premium prices for the gas it needs to keep the lights on through hot summer nights.
nri_angle: Rising energy costs feed into India's broader inflation outlook, affecting household budgets, industrial competitiveness, and the investment environment that NRI investors are watching closely.
